1.0         Introduction
On November 22, 2019, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission or FERC)
issued an Order Granting Authorizations Under Sections 3 and 7 of the Natural Gas Act
(Order) 1, authorizing Rio Grande LNG, LLC, Rio Grande LNG Train 4, LLC and Rio Grande
LNG Train 5, LLC (collectively, “the Rio Grande Entities”) to site, construct, and operate a
natural gas liquefaction facility and liquefied natural gas export terminal (Rio Grande LNG
Terminal or Terminal) in Cameron County, Texas, along the north embankment of the
Brownsville Ship Channel.
This Project Ambient Air Quality Mitigation and Monitoring Plan (Plan) has been developed by
the Rio Grande Entities, in consultation with SLR International Corporation, to fulfill the
requirements of Condition 144 of the FERC Order, as amended for the Terminal. Condition 144
requires the Rio Grande Entities to monitor ambient air quality while conducting simultaneous
construction, commissioning and start-up, and operations with clear thresholds and response
measures tied to the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for particulate matter
less than 2.5 microns (PM2.5), particulate matter less than 10 microns (PM10), and nitrogen
dioxide (NO₂), and to document appropriate mitigation measures in weekly reports.
To meet these obligations, this Plan outlines a comprehensive framework for air quality
monitoring, data management, action level and exceedance response, and reporting. The Plan
leverages a near-reference ambient monitoring system, which has been selected by the Rio
Grande Entities as the preferred system for measuring particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide at
this specific project site. The Plan also incorporates relevant construction-phase mitigation
practices currently implemented to manage particulate emissions.
                              has been identified through collaboration among the Rio Grande
Entities’ environmental staff, Terminal operations and security personnel, nearby landowners,
and third-party contractors. Together, these parties have determined a monitoring location that
provides safe access and representative measurement of impacts from the Terminal during
periods of concurrent activities.
This document details the intended monitoring methodology, equipment specifications, data
handling and reporting procedures, and a suite of mitigation actions that may be required in the
event of exceedances of established thresholds. The Plan also establishes expectations for
periods that monitoring is required and outlines the process for weekly reporting to FERC during
periods when the Plan is active.

1.1         Project Description
The Rio Grande LNG Terminal will be a major liquefied natural gas export facility located along
the Brownsville Ship Channel in Cameron County, Texas, as depicted in Figure 1-1. The
Terminal includes five liquefaction trains, four LNG storage tanks, two ship‑loading berths, a
1,500‑foot turning basin, and support facilities. Site development is well underway, with
substantial construction efforts completed.

1.2         FERC Requirements
Condition 144 of FERC’s 2023 Order on Remand authorization for the Terminal requires the
development and implementation of this Plan. The condition reads as follows:
    “Prior to commissioning, Rio Grande shall file with the Secretary, for review and written
    approval by the Director of the Office of Energy Projects, or the Director’s designee, a
    Project Ambient Air Quality Mitigation and Monitoring Plan for periods when construction,
    commissioning and start-up, and operation of the LNG terminal occur simultaneously. To
    ensure that concurrent emissions during construction, commissioning and start-up, and
    operation of terminal facilities are effectively mitigated, the plan’s thresholds for
    concentrations of particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) and nitrogen oxide (NO2) must be
    established based on the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS), as specified in
    40 CFR Part 50 and shall:
         a. include a monitoring plan for PM2.5, PM10, and NO2, including a description of the site
            selection process for the proposed locations for air quality monitors; data
            management; reporting; and protocols to manage any potential exceedances of the
            NAAQS for PM2.5, PM10, and NO2 that may be observed during the monitoring
            activities;
         b. detail what measures Rio Grande will implement should the levels of PM2.5 or PM10
            exceed the NAAQS 24-hour limit or should the levels of NO2 exceed the NAAQS 1-
            hour limit as specified in 40 CFR Part 50; and
         c. provide that Rio Grande will file weekly reports during periods when the plan is in
            use, documenting the duration of any exceedances, reasons for elevated levels of
            PM2.5, PM10, or NO2, actual measured values, and to the extent there are
            exceedances, what minimization or mitigation measures Rio Grande implemented to
            reduce these levels and documentation of a reduction to or below the threshold(s).”

1.3         Air Quality Thresholds
The Plan’s air quality thresholds were established utilizing the NAAQS as defined in 40 CFR
Part 50. These standards provide the federally recognized thresholds for criteria pollutants,
including PM2.5, PM10, and NO2. The relevant NAAQS used for establishing action thresholds in
this plan include the following:
    •    PM2.5 24-hour standard: 35 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³),
    •    PM10 24-hour standard: 150 µg/m³, and
    •    NO2 1-hour standard: 100 (parts per billion) ppb.
While the Plan utilizes the NAAQS as reference concentrations for establishing project specific
action levels, implementation of this Plan does not constitute a formal NAAQS compliance
demonstration, attainment determination, or regulatory applicability assessment under the Clean
Air Act or 40 CFR Parts 50 and 58. The monitoring conducted pursuant to this Plan is
temporary, project specific, and operational in nature, and is not designed, sited, operated, or
quality assured to meet the regulatory requirements applicable to State and Local Air Monitoring
Stations (SLAMS), NCore, or other EPA ambient air monitoring networks. Such programs have
distinctly different goals, designs, and must be continuously operated for one to three years
depending on form of the NAAQS.

Calibration & Maintenance Schedule
Calibration and maintenance will be performed on time intervals ranging from daily to semi-
annually.
    •    Daily: Automated baseline correction.
    •    Weekly: NO2 zero and span verification.
    •    Monthly: PCX module flow verification.
    •    Quarterly: NO2 module, PCX module, and AirCal 8000 maintenance and calibrations.
    •    Annually: Meteorological sensor exchange.
    •    Every other year: PCX and NO2 module exchange.
These procedures provide data defensibility appropriate for ambient monitoring during
overlapping project activities.

5.0         Data Management, QA/QC, & Reporting
This section outlines the procedures used to ensure all monitoring data are accurate, reliable,
and defensible throughout the project. It describes the data management workflow, validation
and Quality Assurance / Quality Control (QA/QC) checks, and reporting practices. These
processes include automated instrument diagnostics, routine data review, and validation
methods.

5.1         Data Validation Methods
All collected monitoring data will undergo a structured, multi‑tiered validation process to ensure
accuracy, reliability, and defensibility of the dataset. Data validation will follow standard QA/QC
practices used for continuous ambient monitoring programs and will include the following
elements.

Automated System Verification
The AQM65 continuously performs self‑diagnostic checks, including monitoring flow statistics,
baseline evaluations, and system fault detection. On a weekly basis, the NO2 module is
challenged with a two-point calibration check at 0% and 90% of instrument range. Deviation by
more than 20% requires a manual system verification. Automated notifications related to

instrument stability, sensor performance, and any out‑of‑range or non‑physical values are
transmitted to the project team via email or text message.

Manual System Verification
The AQM65 will undergo manual system verification and potential adjustment when automated
system checks vary by more than 20% of target. Additional checks of critical operational
performance criteria, including flow verifications of the particulate sensor will be evaluated to
ensure sufficient flow rate to sample ambient air.

Data Review
Data will be reviewed at least three times weekly for completeness, unusual patterns,
instrument downtime, and meteorological consistency. Any gaps or anomalies (e.g., flat‑lines,
step changes, data spikes) will be flagged for follow‑up review and potential invalidation.

Meteorological Correlation
Wind speed, direction, humidity, and precipitation will be evaluated to determine whether
observed concentration changes are meteorologically consistent with expected dispersion and
transport conditions. Observed concentrations that are inconsistent with contemporaneous
meteorological conditions (e.g., elevated concentrations during upwind or high-dispersion
conditions, or precipitation-driven artifacts) will be flagged for further investigation and may be
invalidated if no plausible source or meteorological explanation is identified.

Manual QA Review
A weekly quality assurance review will be conducted and will include:
    •    Verification of data completeness percentages;
    •    Cross‑checking instrument diagnostic logs, including automated calibration
         assessments;
    •    Confirmation of adherence to calibration schedules; and
    •    Review of exceedance flags and associated field notes.
A QA/QC statement will be included in all reports to FERC documenting data validity.

5.2         Recordkeeping
The Rio Grande Entities, as well as any third-party contractors, will maintain organized records
of all monitoring activities, QA/QC procedures, exceedances, and follow-up actions throughout
periods when construction, commissioning and start-up, and operation occur simultaneously.
Records will be retained for at least five years and stored electronically on secure, controlled
access servers. The following records will be retained.

Monitoring Data & Metadata
    •    All raw and validated pollutant concentration datasets (PM2.5, PM10, NO2)
    •    Time‑stamped meteorological data
    •    Instrument diagnostic logs, fault codes, and uptime statistics

Operation Logs
Environmental staff will maintain digital operation logs documenting:
    •    Construction, commissioning/startup, and operations activities occurring during elevated
         readings;

Exceedance & Follow-up Records
For every exceedance of a PM2.5, PM10, or NO2 action level:

    •    Activity conditions and meteorology at the time;
    •    Investigation findings and source determination; and

5.3         Reporting Frequency
The Rio Grande Entities will provide weekly reports during any period when construction,
commissioning and start-up, and operations occur simultaneously. This is anticipated to first
occur with the commencement of Train 2 commissioning. Each reporting period will cover
Monday through Sunday. The report will be submitted to FERC the week following the end of a
monitoring period, as part of the weekly commissioning report required by Condition 134 of the
Order. Each weekly monitoring report will include:
    •    Summary of PM2.5, PM10, and NO2 concentrations;
    •    Documentation of any exceedances, including measured values and durations;
    •    Evaluation of causes and contributing activities; and
    •    Description of any mitigation measures implemented and confirmation of return to
         below‑threshold conditions, if applicable.

6.0         Action Levels & Mitigation Measures
The action levels are the thresholds that indicate a potential deterioration of air quality and when
project level mitigation measures may be warranted. Action levels for this project are derived
directly from the NAAQS. While the Plan uses the NAAQS as the basis, it does not constitute a
formal NAAQS compliance demonstration or attainment assessment. Instead, the NAAQS serve

as reference values to guide real time monitoring and protective actions during periods when
construction, commissioning/start-up, and operations occur concurrently.

6.1         Action Levels
Action levels for this project are based on selected NAAQS applicable to short‑term evaluations
of ambient air quality. Because the project focuses on near‑field, activity‑related emissions, the
action levels will be set at the NAAQS and managed on the respective averaging periods.
These action levels represent the concentration triggers at which indications of deteriorating air
quality may occur and when project‑level review or mitigation measures may be warranted.
Measured concentrations above the action level or NAAQS do not constitute NAAQS
exceedances. Should concentrations exceed either the 1-hour NO2, 24-hour PM2.5, or 24-hour
PM10 NAAQS, an investigation of site activities will be conducted to determine the cause and
provide recommended corrective action(s). As described in Section 6.2, this review will also
consider external influences that could influence monitored concentrations.

6.2         Corrective Actions & Mitigations
When measured concentrations exceed the action levels as provided in the Plan,
representatives within the Rio Grande Entities who are identified as responsible parties within
the environmental compliance, construction, commissioning and startup, and operational work
groups will be notified. These responsible parties will provide documentation of site activities as
they relate to PM2.5, PM10, or NO2 emissions and will be responsible for implementing any
appropriate mitigations in a timely manner. The Rio Grande Entities and its third-party
contractors will simultaneously conduct an analysis of events and environmental conditions in
the immediate vicinity of the Terminal and monitoring location as well as a review of potential
regional influence that may impact local air quality. This analysis is expected to include but not
necessarily be limited to reviews of:
    •    The concurrent monitored conditions at the TCEQ-operated monitors located on South
         Padre Island as well as in Brownsville;
    •    Prescribed burning activities at nearby US Fish and Wildlife and Texas Parks and
         Wildlife maintained properties (e.g., Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge, Las
         Palomas Wildlife Management Area, etc.);
    •    Wildfires occurring in the region, including those in Mexico;
    •    SpaceX traffic and launch activity; and/or
    •    Any other atypical or exceptional events within the region.
The Rio Grande Entities will be responsible for implementing the appropriate corrective actions
for any site-specific situations identified to potentially contribute to the elevated measured
concentrations at the project-related monitor. The Terminal currently implements the existing
Fugitive Dust Management Plan, which includes through policy and training an anti-idling
requirement for construction contractors and workers (see Accession # 20231004-5074). Each
scenario will be evaluated independently with all potentially contributing causes documented
and addressed as needed. Such actions depend on the equipment and circumstances but may
include:
    •    Reducing or relocating mobile equipment during certain periods,

7.0         Roles & Responsibilities
Prior to the commencement of monitoring activities under this Plan, the responsible parties for
each element will be determined and the responsibilities of the Plan will be clearly
communicated as assigned to the teams and/or individuals with the authority to provide
accurate and timely information as well as enact the necessary mitigation measures.

1.0       Introduction
Rio Grande LNG, LLC (Rio Grande) proposes to construct the Rio Grande liquefied natural gas

2.1        Routine Operations
The proposed Terminal will consist of five liquefaction trains operating simultaneously, each with
a nominal export capacity of 5.4 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) for a total capacity of 27
MTPA. The emission sources listed below will operate continuously, and the air permit

   •   One thermal oxidizer per train;
   •   Two wet/dry gas ground flare system pilot lights [a third standby ground flare system will
       provide redundancy if one of the other units is down and, therefore, is not included in this
       report];
   •   Two condensate storage tanks; and
   •   Fugitive emissions.
The following additional facility emission sources, servicing all five trains, will operate on an
intermittent or as-needed basis:
   •   Maintenance, start up and shutdown emissions controlled by the wet/dry gas ground
       flare systems;
   •   One low-pressure vent with ignition package (warm ship/tank boil-off-gas [BOG]);
   •   Five essential diesel generators;
   •   Two diesel engines for seawater firewater pumps;
   •   LNG vessels;
   •   Tugboats;
   •   Transit/Pilot boat;
   •   USCG Escort vessel; and

2.2         Source Descriptions
2.2.1       Gas Turbines – Refrigeration Compression Gas Turbines
The Terminal will use 10 (two per liquefaction train) General Electric Frame 7 EA gas turbines
for the refrigeration process. These gas turbines will be equipped with dry low NOx burners (5
ppmvd @ 15% O2). Gas turbines are expected to operate full-time throughout the year.

2.2.2       Thermal Oxidizers
There will be five thermal oxidizers at the Terminal facility (one dedicated for each liquefaction
train). Feed natural gas to each liquefaction train will pass through H2S scavenger units to
reduce the hydrogen sulfide content with 90% efficiency. This feed gas stream with most of the
H2S removed will enter the acid gas removal unit where carbon dioxide (CO2) and further H2S
are removed from the feed gas. The waste acid gas stream from the acid gas removal unit is
then sent to the thermal oxidizer for destruction of H2S and hydrocarbons.

2.2.3       Heaters
The Terminal facility will recover waste heat generated by the turbines to regenerate the
dehydration unit’s molecular sieve and heat the hot oil system. Thus, no additional emissions
from process heaters are proposed.

2.2.4       Wet/Dry Gas Flares
There will be three ground flare units at the Terminal facility, with the third unit providing
redundancy if one of the other units is down for maintenance or inspection. The ground flare
units will be 6 feet high and will be enclosed in an approximately 48-foot-high vertical (louvre)
wall for heat protection and to avoid visibility from outside the Terminal.
Each of the ground flares will include both a wet gas header pipe and a dry gas header pipe.
The flare system will be designed to dispose of the maximum anticipated vapor release during a
process unit or site-wide emergency, taking into account all operating modes of the process
units, including startup and shutdown.
The pilot and purge gas (fuel gas) will be operational 8,760 hours per year. A wet (warm) flare
knockout drum will be used to collect water and any free liquids prior to reaching the flare units.
The relief fluids will pass through a dry (cold) flare knockout drum prior to the relief flow reaching
the flare units. The cold liquids collected in the knockout drum will gradually vaporize to the
flare.
The wet and dry ground flares will be used to control maintenance, startup and shutdown (MSS)
emissions. The refrigerant gas compressor turbine maintenance schedule will be used as the
basis for the plant MSS emissions. Three types of maintenance activities occur with different
frequencies as follows:
    •   Combustion path inspection once every 18 months;
    •   Hot gas path inspection once every 36 months; and

During Terminal operation, there is the potential that fugitive emissions from gas and liquid
process streams could be released from piping components, such as from pipe flanges and
valves and other components. A leak detection and repair program will be implemented at the
Terminal.

2.2.9     LNG Vessel and Tugboat Operations
LNG vessel emissions are based on a typical capacity vessel with compression ignition/electric
propulsion. Propulsion emission factors are based on typical vessel engine manufacturer data

Channel (BSC). Emissions are estimated using the number of trips per year and the round-trip

requirements met by auxiliary engines operating solely on marine diesel. Tug emissions are
based upon Tier 4 design standards for the engines on these vessels.

3.2.2     NO2 Modeling Options
Some forms of emitted NOX [i.e., nitrogen oxide (NO)] will react with other atmospheric
constituents (ozone) to form NO2. These reactions are complex and depend on factors such as
mixing of ambient air into the plume, individual reaction rates, and the concentration of specific
reactants in the atmosphere. Regulatory dispersion models such as AERMOD are designed to
model impacts of non-reactive pollutants, but there are various modeling techniques that can be
used to estimate ambient NO2 impacts using these models.
Appendix W presents a three-tiered approach that may be applied to modeling NO2 impacts:
   •    Tier 1 – Assumes 100% conversion of NO to NO2.
   •    Tier 2 – Invokes the Ambient Ratio Method 2 (ARM2) option in AERMOD, which
        provides representative equilibrium ratios of NO2/NOX based on measured ambient
        levels of NO2 and NOX derived from national data from the EPA Air Quality System
        (AQS). Based on the Project’s NOX impacts, a pre-defined portion of NOX is converted to
        NO2
   •    Tier 3 – Uses the ozone limiting method (OLM) or the plume volume molar ratio method
        (PVMRM) as a detailed screening technique.
The Tier 2, ARM2 option in regulatory mode was used in all NO2 model scenarios. The ARM2
option in AERMOD is designed to estimate ambient NO2 concentrations by applying an ambient
ratio of NO2/NOX to the modeled NOX concentration. The NOX concentration is computed by
AERMOD, while the NO2 concentration is estimated by multiplying the NOX concentration with
the ambient ratio.
When run in regulatory mode, AERMOD sets an upper and lower limit of the ambient ratio to 0.9
and 0.5, respectively. This means that the estimated NO2 concentration cannot exceed 90% of
the modeled NOX concentration. Similarly, the lower limit is set at 0.5, ensuring that the
estimated NO2 concentration is at least 50% of the modeled NOX concentration.

3.7        Plume Downwash
The effects of plume downwash were considered for all POINT sources, based on building
locations and heights relative to Terminal emission sources. Direction-specific downwash
parameters were calculated using the current version of the USEPA-approved Building Profile
Input Program (BPIPPRM Version 04274).
In addition to calculating direction-specific building dimensions, the BPIPPRM program also
calculates the Good Engineering Practice (GEP) stack height. The GEP stack height for each
POINT source was calculated pursuant to the USEPA’s methodology to determine “the height
necessary to ensure that emissions from the stack do not result in excessive concentrations of
any air pollutant in the immediate vicinity of the source as a result of atmospheric downwash,
eddies or wakes which may be created by the source itself, nearby structures or nearby terrain
obstacles.”
Pursuant to 40 CFR 51.100(ii), the GEP stack height is defined as the greater of:
   •   65 meters, measured from the ground-level elevation at the base of the stack; or
   •   Hg = H + 1.5L, where:
       o   Hg = good engineering practice stack height, measured from the ground-level
           elevation at the base of the stack,

Availability of valid data
For an air quality monitoring station to be used in a NAAQS analysis, EPA established
Monitoring Quality Objectives with Systematic Criteria (QA Handbook Volume II, Appendix D,
PM2.5 Filter Based Local Condition Validation Template, Rev. No. 1, March 2017 and the ADEC
AM&QA QAPP April, 2018) including a data completeness of at least 75% for each calendar
year quarter and 90% of the days within a year. This requirement ensures that the data
collected is representative and reliable for making regulatory decisions (i.e., meets data quality
objectives set in 40 CFR 58. When data collection does not meet these criteria, values can
skew in either direction for reasons unrelated to the environmental factors that contribute to the
real levels in the air. This also prevents seasonal biases from unduly influencing the final values.
For example, the primary annual standard for PM2.5 is 9 µg/m3, but specifically, it is the annual
arithmetic mean (average), averaged over a three-year period. For this reason, “valid data” from
a monitoring station is considered to be three years (ideally consecutive) of valid data. An
evaluation of the availability of valid data is typically the first, and often the only, significant point
of analysis in determining the viability of a monitor for use in contributing background data to an
analysis. In prior modeling demonstrations conducted for the Project, the lack of availability of
valid data has resulted in changes of the utilized air quality station – particularly for PM2.5, where
two such potential stations were at times available.

Location with respect to project site and anticipated impacts
The proximity of a monitoring site to a proposed project location can be both a valuable trait but
also a misleading characteristic in areas with variable land use such as the location of the
Project. When possible, choosing an ambient air monitor in the vicinity of the project allows for
the monitor to typically capture the same background air as is expected to be found at the
project site itself. The monitor is expected to experience approximately the same wind speeds
and patterns and see variability in the same general time and space as would the air at the
project site. This is truer when the terrain and the meteorological patterns are generally
consistent, as opposed to areas with significant terrain or other features (e.g. mountains or
dense urban areas). Changing meteorological patterns along the coast can also decrease the
distance at which a monitor site could be reasonably representative of a project site given the
variability of speed and direction from land-sea breezes.

Potential influence of local sources
40 CFR 51, Appendix W guides the selection of data used to represent the background when
predicting cumulative impacts. It specifically notes at the start of its discussion of background
concentrations that “Background air quality should not include the ambient impacts of the
project source under consideration”. Nearby sources should be explicitly included in the
modeling inventory specifically when they are not adequately represented by ambient
monitoring data. When evaluating a monitoring station for its use in a NAAQS analysis, care
must be taken to ensure that sources are accounted for once, specifically, either as captured in

needs to be able to represent regional anthropogenic and natural sources that are not and

mobile source emissions from local and regional traffic. As best as possible, the ambient station
needs to represent the concentrations that arise as a result of these typical man-made and
natural sources while not double counting the emissions from the project in question or other
stationary sources. Exceptional events, such as sustained wildfires and industrial accidental
releases can also influence the measurements made at a particular monitoring station. The
impact of these events needs to be analyzed and generally removed from the data set in
question.

Monitoring scale and objective
Certain monitors are placed in order to achieve specific monitoring goals. Some monitors, such
as those ideal for providing background monitor data for this purpose, are placed to collect data
on regional or urban scales. An urban scale monitor for fine particulate matter is designed to
capture the concentration of a particular pollutant on the order of 4-50 km, generally the size of
a metropolitan area. These monitors can accurately assess trends that occur within this space
and can be used to evaluate control strategies on a larger scale. Regional monitors cover
hundreds of kilometers and are effective at characterizing pollutant transport as well as large
scale emissions and losses. On the other end of the scale, some monitors are placed in such a
way as to specifically capture the emissions from a single source, or the contributions of
sources over a smaller area like a neighborhood. The values these monitors measure on the
microscale or middle scale are potentially reflective of a single industrial facility or highway
interchange. These monitors provide valuable data for a small area around their location but are
not particularly reflective of the average concentrations of a particular pollutant within a broader
space.

Previous use for modeling projects conducted within the proposed modeling domain
Previous approval of the use of a particular background monitoring station from past air quality
demonstrations conducted within the proposed modeling domain (i.e. the area around which the
impacts from the proposed project will be evaluated) are useful historical tools to review in
determining the adequacy and representativeness of a background monitor location. In this
particular case, no such analyses were considered or relevant. However, the consideration and
potential evaluation of that historical usage is often a factor in determining site
representativeness, and thus it is included here for completeness.
Two primary controlling factors that can change in the evaluation of monitoring stations are the
availability of valid data from year to year and the influence of local sources (either positive or
negative) on the monitor’s measured values. In this case, historical information was not used to
evaluate the monitoring stations because the representativeness determination was conducted
from scratch. Each particular project and its specifics requires that professional judgement be
applied to weigh the criteria and their relative importance in selecting a site for ambient
background data. In general, the monitoring site should be similar to the project site in terms of
terrain features and meteorological patterns. The sites need not be as close as available in
terms of distance – in fact, it is possible to select a monitoring station based outside the
modeling domain entirely depending on the representativeness of the available sites. It is
important to avoid background monitor data that is overly influenced by the project site and
existing sources, because it no longer serves its intended purpose as an actual background.

Facilities conducting air quality analyses under the requirements that stem from the Clean Air
Act are generally focused on the comparison of modeling results to the applicable ambient
standards, per pollutant and averaging period. This demonstration includes such a numerical
comparison, which does show that the facility does not cause or contribute to an exceedance of
any NAAQS. There is a distinction, however, between the definition of significant impact and
cumulative effects as represented under the Clean Air Act and as defined under NEPA. NEPA’s
evaluation of the cumulative impact of a project is required to account for the context and
intensity of an effect of a proposed action. A NAAQS analysis conducted and submitted may not
explicitly summarize the potential impacts on these factors, but the NAAQS itself is a public
health standard designed to protect the entire population, including sensitive subgroups. This
includes environmental justice communities, sensitive areas based on cultural and historical
significance, ecologically sensitive areas, and areas with special visibility concerns. Federal
agencies have long accepted a valid NAAQS compliance demonstration as a sufficient
demonstration with respect to air quality that the environment will not be adversely affected
under NEPA.
EPA’s use of significant impact levels is intended to set a numerical standard below which the
assessment of additional environmental impacts is not necessary – a reduction in the
complexity of the analysis of the ambient air impacts from a given project, since the best
scientific understanding of the modeled concentrations for a given pollutant and averaging
period has shown in such a situation that there are not measurable impacts below that level.
That a facility is shown not to cause or contribute to a violation of the standard is to state
succinctly that the contributions as modeled from the facility do not have a statistically
meaningful impact on the overall modeled results, whether or not that total number is shown to
be above or below that particular standard.
